figures.alt: Illustration of two teams of teenagers pulling on a rope in a tug of war. The red ribbon at the middle of the rope has not moved from the center.
figures.caption: Equal pulls in opposite directions are balanced. The rope does not change its motion.

figures.alt: Photo of a red horseshoe magnet holding two steel paper clips. A penny and a piece of aluminum foil lie beside it, not touching it.
figures.caption: A magnet pulls steel paper clips. The penny and the foil do not stick.

figures.alt: Two pictures of an object with force arrows. Top: a push forward and friction backward are the same length, so the forces are balanced and the object keeps moving at the same steady speed. Bottom: the push forward is longer than the friction arrow, so the forces are unbalanced and the object speeds up.
figures.caption: Balanced forces do not change motion. An object can be moving and still have balanced forces. Unbalanced forces change the motion.

figures.alt: Side view. A cardboard sheet rests like a bridge on two stacks of books. A paper clip sits on top of the cardboard at the start line. A magnet is held under the cardboard and moved along, and the clip follows it toward the finish line, at least 20 centimeters away. Nobody touches the clip.
figures.caption: What the paper-clip mover kit looks like from the side.

figures.alt: Two dot tapes, each showing a ball position every second from 0 to 4 seconds. Top, a model ball with no friction: the dots are equally far apart, so the speed is steady. Bottom, a real ball on a floor: the gaps between dots get smaller each second, so the ball is slowing down, and friction pushes against the motion. Close dots mean slow and far apart dots mean fast.
figures.caption: Equal gaps between dots mean steady speed. A real ball on a floor slows down, so its dots bunch closer together.

figures.alt: Line graph of a model ball with no friction. Position is 0 cm at 0 s, 10 at 1 s, 20 at 2 s, 30 at 3 s, in a straight line. The prediction for 4 s is 40 cm, shown as an open dot.
figures.caption: Backup set 1 for a model ball with no friction: 0, 10, 20 and 30 cm at 0, 1, 2 and 3 seconds. The open dot is the prediction, 40 cm at 4 seconds. A real ball on a floor slows down, so its dots would bunch closer.

figures.alt: Line graph. Position is 0 cm at 0 s, 8 at 1 s, 16 at 2 s, 24 at 3 s, in a straight line. The prediction for 4 s is 32 cm, shown as an open dot.
figures.caption: Backup set 2: 0, 8, 16 and 24 cm at 0, 1, 2 and 3 seconds. The open dot predicts 32 cm at 4 seconds.
